1H (Number Theory)

Words: 73 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 73
1H OurBigBook.com
For every prime factor pi​ of N, Fermat's little theorem gives api​−1≡1(modpi​). Since pi​−1 divides the least common multiple λ(N), it follows that pi​∣aλ(N)−1. The primes are distinct and hence pairwise coprime, so their product divides this integer. Thus
aλ(N)≡1(modN).​
(1)
For the specified product, N=1729 and λ(N)=lcm(6,12,18)=36. Since N−1=1728=48⋅36, raising the preceding modular congruence to the forty-eighth power proves aN−1≡1(modN) for every a coprime to N. This is the defining phenomenon of a Carmichael number.

2G OurBigBook.com
Introduce p−1​=1, q−1​=0, p0​=a0​ and q0​=1. Composition of the Möbius transformations z↦aj​+1/z represents a finite continued fraction. Their matrices give
(pn​qn​​pn−1​qn−1​​)=(a0​1​10​)(a1​1​10​)⋯(an​1​10​).​
(2)
Indeed, multiplying the last factor gives the linear recurrences pn​=an​pn−1​+pn−2​ and qn​=an​qn−1​+qn−2​, which reproduce the continued fraction convergents of the continued fraction. Each factor has determinant −1. Taking determinants therefore yields
pn​qn−1​−qn​pn−1​=(−1)n+1.​
(3)
This identity also proves that the numerator and denominator in the first column are coprime, so no unnoticed cancellation changes the displayed matrix.

3F (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 288 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 288
3F OurBigBook.com
Extend the Möbius transformations to isometries of three-dimensional hyperbolic space. For any interior point o, the limit set of a Kleinian group is the set of boundary accumulation points of Go. Its definition is independent of o: two interior orbits stay at a bounded hyperbolic distance, so have the same boundary limits. The Kleinian limit set is closed and G-invariant. Iterating a loxodromic Möbius transformation in the positive and negative directions shows that its two fixed points belong to the Kleinian limit set.
The two fixed-point sets in this problem cannot have exactly one common point. Otherwise conjugate that point to infinity and the other fixed point of the first transformation to zero. The transformations then have the forms f(z)=αz, with ∣α∣>1, and g(z)=βz+b, with b=0. But f−ngfn(z)=βz+bα−n is a sequence of distinct group elements converging in the Möbius group. Taking quotients of consecutive elements gives nonidentity elements converging to the identity, contrary to discrete subgroup. Consequently the Kleinian limit set contains at least three points.
Let ξ be any point of the Kleinian limit set, and choose distinct gn​ with gn​o→ξ. The rank-one convergence of divergent Möbius transformations supplies a subsequence converging to ξ uniformly away from one exceptional boundary point η. To see the lemma directly, normalize determinant-one representing matrices by their norms. The norms tend to infinity, and a subsequential limit has rank one: its kernel is η and its image is the attracting point. In the positive-Hermitian-matrix model of hyperbolic space, gn​o has this same image limit, so the attracting point is indeed ξ.
Choose distinct ζ1​,ζ2​ in the Kleinian limit set other than η. Then gn​ζ1​ and gn​ζ2​ both tend to ξ, belong to the Kleinian limit set, and remain distinct because gn​ is injective. If ξ were isolated, both would eventually equal ξ, an impossibility. The limit set has no isolated points.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 141
4G OurBigBook.com
A binary block code is a subset C⊆{0,1}n; its length is the common word length n, its size is m=∣C∣, and its minimum distance is the least Hamming distance between distinct words. There are V(n,r)=∑j=0r​(jn​) words in a radius-r Hamming ball, since one chooses the positions to change.
Put t=⌊(d−1)/2⌋. Two radius-t Hamming balls about different codewords cannot meet: otherwise the triangle inequality would make their centres at distance at most 2t<d. Comparing their combined size with 2n gives the Hamming bound
A(n,d)V(n,t)≤2n.
(4)
For the other direction, start with one word and repeatedly add any word at distance at least d from every word already selected. Finiteness ensures that this process stops. At that point the radius-(d−1) Hamming balls cover the entire cube; an uncovered word could otherwise be added. These balls may overlap, but their total size is at least 2n. This gives the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
V(n,d−1)2n​≤A(n,d)≤V(n,⌊(d−1)/2⌋)2n​.​
(5)

In a generalized linear model, the linear predictor is ηi​=xiT​β, a linear combination of the covariates with unknown coefficients. The link function relates this predictor to the mean: g(μi​)=ηi​. The canonical link function chooses the natural parameter of the exponential family, namely g(μ)=θ(μ). Differentiating the normalization of the density shows that μ=K′(θ), so the canonical link function is (K′)−1 on the admissible parameter interval.
For a Bernoulli distribution, the probability mass function can be written as
μy(1−μ)1−y=exp{ylog1−μμ​+log(1−μ)}.
(6)
Thus θ=log(μ/(1−μ)) and K(θ)=log(1+eθ). The canonical link is the logit:
g(μ)=log1−μμ​,0<μ<1.​
(7)

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 261 Articles: 5
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 88
6B OurBigBook.com
The infection term rIS is a mass-action contact rate: each infection removes one susceptible individual and adds one infected individual. Recovery at rate aI transfers individuals from the infected class to the recovered class. Loss of immunity at rate pR transfers recovered individuals back to the susceptible class. Thus these equations describe the SIR model with waning immunity, also called the SIRS model. Adding the equations gives S˙+I˙+R˙=0, so S+I+R=N. The nonnegative population region is invariant because the derivative of any population on its zero boundary is nonnegative.

a

Words: 34 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 34
a OurBigBook.com
Since S≤N, the infected population satisfies I˙=(rS−a)I≤(rN−a)I. Integration gives I(t)≤I(0)e(rN−a)t. Hence rN<a forces the infected population to decrease exponentially from the outset: there is no epidemic outbreak.

b

Words: 139 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 139
b OurBigBook.com
For rN>a and p>0, a nonzero infected equilibrium requires S∗​=a/r. Using aI∗​=pR∗​ and population conservation gives
S∗​=ra​,I∗​=a+pp​(N−ra​),R∗​=a+pa​(N−ra​).​
(8)
Eliminate R=N−S−I before assessing stability, since perturbations must preserve the total population. The resulting Jacobian matrix at this endemic equilibrium is
J=(−p−rI∗​rI∗​​−p−a0​),trJ=−a+pp(p+rN)​,detJ=p(rN−a).
(9)
Its trace is negative and its determinant positive, so both eigenvalues have negative real part: the endemic equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable on the fixed-population plane. The full three-variable system has a neutral direction corresponding to changing the conserved population.
Writing κ=rN−a>0, as p→0 the trace is −prN/a+O(p2) and the determinant is pκ. Hence the discriminant (trJ)2−4detJ=−4pκ+O(p2)<0. As p→∞, the trace is −p−κ+O(p−1) and the determinant is again pκ, giving a positive discriminant p2+O(p). Both quantities are O(p) in both limits, but the eigenvalues are complex for sufficiently small p and real for sufficiently large p.

Representative normal forms are x˙=μ+x2 for a saddle-node bifurcation, x˙=μx−x2 for a transcritical bifurcation, and x˙=μx−x3 for a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. Replacing the last cubic term by +x3 gives the subcritical pitchfork bifurcation.
Treat μ as a variable with μ˙​=0. The extended center manifold is tangent to y=0, so write y=h(x,μ)=Ax2+Bxμ+Cμ2+O((∣x∣+∣μ∣)3). Its invariance equation is hx​x˙=y˙​. At quadratic order this reads
(2Ax+Bμ)μ=(2−A)x2−Bxμ−Cμ2.
(10)
Matching coefficients gives A=2, B=−4, C=4. Substitution into the first equation therefore gives
y=2x2−4xμ+4μ2+O(3),x˙=μ+x2−4xμ+4μ2+O(3).​
(11)
Here O(3) denotes total degree at least three in (x,μ). With T=t, X=x−2μ and μ​=μ, this becomes dX/dT=μ​+X2+O(3). Thus α=1, β=2, γ(μ)=μ, and the bifurcation is a saddle-node. For negative parameter, the negative-X branch is stable and the positive-X branch unstable along the center manifold; the transverse eigenvalue is near −1.

For real b=0, the integrand depends only on b2, so first take b>0. Integrate eiz/(z2−b2) over the upper-half-plane semicircle, indenting above both real poles with small clockwise semicircles. The large arc tends to zero by Jordan lemma. Each indentation contributes −iπ times its residue, and there are no enclosed poles. Thus the Cauchy principal value on the whole real axis is
PV∫−∞∞​u2−b2eiu​du=iπ(2beib​−2be−ib​)=−bπsinb​.
(12)
The imaginary part is odd and the real part even. Taking the real part and halving gives
PV∫0∞​u2−b2cosu​du=−2bπsinb​.​
(13)
The right-hand side is even in b, completing the negative-b case as well.

The bob has x˙=ℓcosθθ˙ and y˙​=at−ℓsinθθ˙. Substituting these into the Lagrangian gives
L=21​mℓ2θ˙2−maℓtsinθθ˙+mgℓcosθ+21​m(a2+ga)t2.
(14)
The mixed term is dtd​(maℓtcosθ)−maℓcosθ. Removing this total derivative and the time-only term leaves the equivalent Lagrangian Leff​=21​mℓ2θ˙2+m(g−a)ℓcosθ. The Euler-Lagrange equation becomes
θ¨+ℓg−a​sinθ=0.​
(15)
In free fall, a=g, so θ=θ0​+ω0​t: a bob initially at rest relative to the lift remains at its initial angle, and otherwise moves around the pivot with constant angular speed. Every constant angle is then an equilibrium, with no restoring force. For a=g, the equilibria are θ=0 and θ=π modulo 2π.

Near θ=0, the linearized equation is θ¨+(g−a)θ/ℓ=0. When a<g this is an harmonic oscillator, so the downward configuration is stable. Writing θ=π+ε instead gives ε¨−(g−a)ε/ℓ=0, with an exponentially growing solution. Downward is stable; upward is unstable.

a OurBigBook.com
A thin spherical shell has mass 4πr2ρdr and inward gravitational force Gm(r)(4πr2ρdr)/r2. The net outward pressure force is −4πr2P′(r)dr. Their balance gives the hydrostatic equilibrium equation
P′=−r2Gmρ​.​
(16)
Since m′=4πr2ρ, multiplying by r2/ρ and differentiating yields drd​(r2P′/ρ)=−4πGr2ρ.
At the centre, require m(0)=0 and finite P(0) and ρ(0). Spherical symmetry gives P′(0)=0; indeed m(r)=O(r3) makes the pressure gradient O(r) for regular density. At the surface require P(R)=Pext​, usually approximated by zero, because pressure matches the surrounding medium. If the stellar mass is prescribed, also impose m(R)=M. An equation of state is needed to close the system. A vanishing surface density is appropriate for some stellar models but is not a universal boundary condition.

b

Words: 165 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 165
b OurBigBook.com
After its giant phases, the Sun ejects much of its envelope and leaves a carbon–oxygen white dwarf. The remnant mass lies below the Chandrasekhar limit. Its support is chiefly electron degeneracy pressure: the Pauli exclusion principle forces electrons into distinct momentum states even at low temperature, giving P∝ρ5/3 when they are nonrelativistic. Consequently pressure support need not cease when nuclear burning ends. The white dwarf subsequently cools and fades.
The process called inverse beta decay here is electron capture, e−+p→n+νe​, becomes possible for free particles when the electron's total energy exceeds approximately (mn​−mp​)c2≃2.6me​c2, corresponding to a kinetic energy about 1.6me​c2. Electron capture on nuclei has thresholds modified by nuclear binding energies. In a solar-mass progenitor's ordinary white dwarf remnant, the Fermi energy is below the relevant capture thresholds, so the electron population providing support is stable. At much higher density, electron capture can reduce the electron density and pressure and promote collapse; this is why stability against electron capture matters in assessing degeneracy support. The Sun ends as a cooling white dwarf, rather than a neutron star.

11H (Number Theory)

Words: 193 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 193
11H OurBigBook.com
The Prime number theorem states that π(x)∼x/logx, where π(x) counts primes not exceeding x. Dirichlet theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions states that if gcd(a,m)=1, then the progression a+jm contains infinitely many primes.
If x2≡−1(modp) for an odd prime p, the multiplicative order of x modulo p is four. Lagrange's theorem therefore gives 4∣p−1. Conversely, Wilson's theorem gives (p−1)!≡−1(modp). Pairing the factors j and p−j yields
(−1)(p−1)/2((2p−1​)!)2≡−1(modp).
(17)
For p≡1(mod4), the sign is positive, so the factorial supplies a square root of −1. Thus −1 is a quadratic residue exactly when p≡1(mod4).
Write P=∏j​pj​. The odd integer 4P−1 is 3 modulo 4. If all of its prime factors were 1 modulo 4, their product, with multiplicities, would be 1 modulo 4, so at least one factor is 3 modulo 4. Every prime factor q of 4P2+1 is odd and satisfies (2P)2≡−1(modq); the criterion just proved gives q≡1(mod4). Neither integer is divisible by any pj​, since their residues modulo pj​ are respectively −1 and 1. Starting with any finite list thus produces a new prime in each residue class. Both classes contain infinitely many primes, independently of the general Dirichlet theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.

12G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 427 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 427
12G OurBigBook.com
In the RSA cryptosystem, choose distinct large primes p,q, put N=pq, choose e coprime to φ(N)=(p−1)(q−1), and choose d with ed≡1(modφ(N)). Publish (N,e) and keep the factorization and d private. Encrypt a properly encoded message M as C=MemodN and decrypt as M=CdmodN. The Chinese remainder theorem proves correctness even for nonunits: modulo either prime, the message is either zero or satisfies Fermat's little theorem.
The public exponent 65537=216+1 has few nonzero binary digits, so exponentiation needs only sixteen squarings and one extra multiplication. It is an efficient conventional choice, subject to the required coprimality and secure randomized message encoding. The same numerical choice for the private exponent would speed decryption, but for large moduli with balanced prime factors it is disastrously small: the continued-fraction attack on a small RSA private exponent recovers d when, for example, d<31​N1/4 and q<p<2q. A small public exponent and a small private exponent have very different security implications.
To factor N from e,d, write ed−1=2st with t odd. Choose random a modulo N. If gcd(a,N) is nontrivial, factoring is already done. Otherwise compute b=at and repeatedly square; the final value is one. If a value x immediately preceding the first one is neither 1 nor −1 modulo N, then x2≡1(modN) and
gcd(x−1,N) is a nontrivial factor of N.​
(18)
Indeed, the signs of x modulo p and q differ. Restart if the chain begins at one or reaches −1 first. The Chinese remainder theorem makes the two prime components independent for a uniformly chosen unit. Their two-primary orders differ with probability at least one half: if the two exponents of two in p−1,q−1 are equal, the probability of equal orders is at most one half, and if unequal it is smaller. Since odd t preserves these orders, this gives a randomized factoring procedure with bounded expected repetitions.
A bit commitment must be hiding before opening and binding after it. A concrete RSA construction uses a valid public RSA permutation whose inverse is unavailable to the receiver. Choose a random unit x and a random bit vector r, and set h(x,r) to their binary inner product modulo two. Send y=xemodN, r, and c=b⊕h(x,r). To open, reveal x; the receiver checks xe=y and recovers b=c⊕h(x,r). Injectivity makes the opening bit unique. The hard-core predicate theorem applied to (x,r)↦(xe,r) gives computational hiding under the RSA inversion assumption. The setup must ensure a valid modulus and exponent without giving the receiver the private exponent; otherwise hiding fails. Merely encrypting 0 or 1 would not hide a bit, since both ciphertexts could be computed publicly.

A homogeneous equilibrium has v0​=u02​. Besides u0​=0, a nonzero equilibrium satisfies r=u02​−u0​, giving u±​=(1±1+4r​)/2. Concentrations are nonnegative, so only nonnegative roots are physically admissible. At a positive equilibrium, the reaction Jacobian matrix is
J=(u0​2su0​​−u0​−s​),trJ=u0​−s,detJ=su0​(2u0​−1).
(19)
Negative trace and positive determinant are equivalent to
21​<u0​<s.​
(20)
Thus a positive homogeneous stable branch exists precisely when s>1/2 and −1/4<r<s2−s, on the upper root u+​. The lower positive branch has negative determinant and is unstable. At r=−1/4 the branches meet and have a zero eigenvalue; at u0​=s the strict linear stability condition also fails.
The trivial equilibrium (0,0) has eigenvalues r,−s, so it is asymptotically stable for r<0. It exists for all r, independently of the nonzero branches. If negative u0​ were allowed mathematically, the negative branch for r>0 would also be homogeneously stable, but it does not represent a chemical concentration.

A Fourier mode with q=k2≥0 evolves under J−qdiag(κ1​,κ2​). Its trace remains negative for a homogeneously stable positive branch. Its determinant is
D(q)=κ1​κ2​q2+(sκ1​−u0​κ2​)q+s(2u02​−u0​).
(21)
If u0​κ2​≤sκ1​, this is positive for every q≥0. Otherwise its minimum is attained at q∗​=(u0​κ2​−sκ1​)/(2κ1​κ2​). Stability requires D(q∗​)>0, or
u0​κ2​−sκ1​<2κ1​κ2​s(2u02​−u0​)​.
(22)
In terms of d=κ2​/κ1​​, the boundary is the positive root of u0​d2−s=2ds(2u02​−u0​)​:
dc​(u0​)=2s​+u0​s(2u02​−u0​)​​.​
(23)
Within 1/2<u0​<s, all modes decay for d<dc​; a finite band grows for d>dc​, giving a Turing instability. Equality is neutral at one nonzero wavenumber.
For s=2, the positive lower branch 0<u0​<1/2 is unstable for every d. The upper branch is homogeneously stable for 1/2<u0​<2: it is stable to all modes to the left of dc​=2+4−2/u0​​ and unstable to spatial modes to the right. For u0​>2 it is already homogeneously unstable. The zero branch is stable to every spatial mode when r<0, because its mode eigenvalues are r−κ1​k2 and −s−κ2​k2.

At onset the determinant has a double root, so
kc2​=2κ1​κ2​u0​κ2​−sκ1​​=2dκ1​κ2​​u0​d2−s​.
(24)
Squaring the neutral-boundary equation and canceling the positive factors gives u0​=s/[d(22s​−d)]. Substitution yields
kc2​=κ1​κ2​​1​d(22s​−d)s(d−2s​)​.​

For a positive branch with u0​>1/2, the actual neutral curve lies strictly between 2s​ and 22s​. If d<2s​, then d<dc​(u0​) for every such branch: a homogeneously stable state cannot have this Turing instability. If d>22s​, then d>dc​(u0​) for every finite positive u0​, so every homogeneously stable positive state is spatially unstable. The negative value yielded by the displayed formula outside its boundary domain is not a physical critical wavenumber and does not imply renewed stability. One must also keep u0​<s, which can restrict the attainable neutral curve further.

Write the Papperitz symbol by listing pairs of exponents at 0,1,∞. For F(a,c−b;c;w) they are (0,1−c), (0,b−a), and (a,c−b). Under w=z/(z−1) the points 0,1,∞ in the z-plane correspond respectively to 0,∞,1 in the w-plane. Thus the pulled-back exponents are (0,1−c) at zero, (a,c−b) at one, and (0,b−a) at infinity.
Multiplication by (1−z)−a shifts the exponents at one by −a and those at infinity by +a, yielding
P⎩⎨⎧​001−c​10c−a−b​∞ab​z​⎭⎬⎫​.
(26)
This is the original Gauss hypergeometric equation. Both functions are analytic and normalized to one at zero, so uniqueness of that normalized local solution proves the Pfaff transformation
F(a,b;c;z)=(1−z)−aF(a,c−b;c;z−1z​).​
(27)
Continue the identity using the branch ∣arg(1−z)∣<π. As usual, the parameters must admit the normalized hypergeometric solution; excluded singular parameter values are treated only when their limiting solution exists.

A first-order structure consists of a nonempty domain, an interpretation of each constant as a domain element, each k-ary function symbol as a map from the k-fold domain product to the domain, and each k-ary relation symbol as a subset of that product. Under an assignment of values to variables, terms are evaluated recursively. Atomic formulas assert equality of term values or membership in an interpreted relation. Boolean connectives act on truth values, and quantifiers range over the whole domain. The set [[φ]]A​ consists of assignments to the free variables making the formula true.
For a substructure B⊆A, constants lie in B, functions restrict to B, and relations restrict to tuples from B. Induction on terms shows that every term with arguments from B has the same value in both structures. Atomic formulas consequently have the same truth values, and induction on Boolean connectives gives
[[φ]]B​=[[φ]]A​∩Bn​

for every quantifier-free formula.
For a nonempty chain of T-model substructures, form their union U. Every finite tuple belongs to one member of the chain, so U is closed under all interpreted functions and contains the constants. Consider any inductive axiom ∀x∃yψ(x,y). A specified finite tuple x lies in one member, which supplies witnesses y there. The quantifier-free formula ψ has the same truth value in that member and U, so U satisfies the axiom. Hence U is a T-model and the least upper bound of the chain. The poset is complete for nonempty chains. If chain-complete is defined to include the empty chain, a least element must additionally exist, which the stated hypotheses do not ensure.

20H (Algebraic Topology)

Solution

20H OurBigBook.com
The fundamental group of the figure-eight is the free group on its two circle loops a,b. A two-sheeted covering space is specified by their permutations of the two-point fiber. It is connected exactly when this action is transitive, equivalently when at least one permutation exchanges the sheets. Since S2​ is abelian, relabeling the two sheets does not identify any further cases. There are therefore three connected double covers, given by (a,b)=(τ,1),(1,τ),(τ,τ), where τ exchanges the sheets.
In either of the first two covers there are two vertices joined by two parallel edges, with a loop at each vertex. The two covers differ as covers of the fixed base, but their total spaces are homeomorphic by exchanging the base-circle labels. The third cover has two vertices joined by four parallel edges and no loops.
These last two graph types are not homeomorphic. Their two degree-four branch points are intrinsically identifiable topologically. Removing either branch point in the graph with loops leaves two components: the punctured loop at that point, and the remaining connected graph. Removing either branch point in the four-edge graph leaves a connected four-armed graph. Thus the three covers give two homeomorphism types of total space. This is the distinction between equivalence of covers and homeomorphism of covering spaces.

Complete the random assignment by assigning passenger N to the one vacant seat. This turns the uniformly random seating of the first N−1 passengers into a uniformly random permutation of all N passengers. Following an occupant to the seat on their ticket traverses precisely the cycle containing N; the process ends at the initially vacant seat.
The cycle length of a tagged element in a uniform permutation is uniform on {1,…,N}. Indeed, for length ℓ, its count is (ℓ−1N−1​)(ℓ−1)!(N−ℓ)!=(N−1)!, out of N! equally likely permutations. A cycle of length ℓ displaces ℓ−1 already-seated passengers. The mean number of displacements is therefore (N−1)/2. Conditional on the cycle, summing the mean duration μ−1 of each displacement gives
E(displacement delay)=2μN−1​.​
(42)
This counts the delay caused by moving already-seated passengers, as the final wording suggests. If “each move” is intended also to charge the last passenger's own initial seating, even when their seat was vacant, the number of timed moves is ℓ instead, and the answer is (N+1)/(2μ). These conventions differ by the baseline boarding time μ−1; the distinction is present in the source wording.

In Bayesian inference, a finite parameter space has posterior probabilities π(θ)=w(θ)/Z, with w(θ) the product of the prior probability and likelihood and Z=∑θ​w(θ) the evidence. Although each weight may be easy to evaluate, summing a large parameter space can be impractical. The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm constructs a Markov chain with posterior stationary distribution, allowing posterior expectations, probabilities and credible regions to be estimated from its trajectory. Its acceptance ratios cancel Z, so direct enumeration of the normalizing constant is unnecessary. Posterior sampling alone does not automatically provide the evidence for comparing models.

(43)
Otherwise stay at θ. For distinct states, the accepted transition kernel satisfies
π(θ)P(θ,θ′)=min{π(θ)q(θ,θ′),π(θ′)q(θ′,θ)}=π(θ′)P(θ′,θ).
(44)
Thus detailed balance holds, and summing over θ proves stationarity. Irreducibility of the accepted kernel makes this stationary distribution unique. Proposal irreducibility by itself is insufficient if proposed edges have zero reverse probability and are always rejected.
For convergence of the distribution from an arbitrary start, also require aperiodicity, which can always be supplied by making the chain lazy. In a finite irreducible aperiodic chain, some power Pm has all entries positive. Its rows then share a fixed positive probability component, so repeated application contracts total variation distance geometrically. This proves that the chain's distribution approaches π.
The stronger fact needed for averages is
M1​j=1∑M​h(Θj​)⟶θ∑​π(θ)h(θ)almost surely.​
(45)
One can justify this directly by returns to a chosen state. Successive excursions are independent identically distributed cycles by the Strong Markov property. In a finite irreducible chain, return times have finite mean: from every state there is a path of uniformly bounded length and uniformly positive probability to the chosen state, giving a geometric tail bound. Apply the strong law of large numbers to cycle lengths and accumulated rewards. Their ratio converges; the mean visits per cycle, normalized by the mean cycle length, form a stationary distribution and hence equal π. The unfinished final cycle is negligible. This proves the displayed average law, even when the chain is periodic. Under these conditions, Metropolis–Hastings delivers the required posterior expectations.

The proposal must connect the whole positive posterior support by moves with nonzero reverse probability. Use the full Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability for asymmetric proposals; dropping the reverse proposal factor generally targets the wrong distribution. Compute likelihoods and acceptance ratios on a logarithmic scale to avoid overflow and underflow, and handle zero weights explicitly. A lazy step prevents periodicity when distributional convergence is needed.
Finite-chain convergence does not guarantee a useful run length: separated modes and narrow bottlenecks can make mixing extremely slow. Tune proposals to explore efficiently, inspect several starting points and chains, and assess autocorrelation and Monte Carlo uncertainty rather than treating correlated draws as independent observations. Discarding an initial segment can reduce initialization effects, but diagnostics do not prove that every posterior mode has been visited. Thinning is not required for correctness and often throws away useful information. The model and prior must themselves be specified correctly; an exact sampler from an incorrect posterior cannot repair the model.

Let Ht​(x)=(4πt)−n/2e−∣x∣2/(4t) be the heat kernel, and write Pt​g=Ht​∗g. The homogeneous solution is u(t,x)=Pt​g(x): differentiation verifies the heat equation, and the approximate-identity property recovers the smooth initial data.
The Duhamel principle gives
v(t,x)=Pt​g(x)+∫0t​Pt−s​f(s,⋅)(x)ds.​
(55)
Each source impulse at time s evolves by the homogeneous heat flow for duration t−s. More formally, differentiating the time integral gives f(t,x)+∫0t​ΔPt−s​f(s)(x)ds. Subtracting its Laplacian leaves f. The integral tends to zero as t↓0, since its absolute value is at most tsups≤t​∥f(s)∥∞​. Thus the initial condition is also correct. Smoothness permits differentiation locally; standard cutoff or semigroup arguments justify it for bounded smooth data without global bounds on all derivatives.
For n=4 and time-independent Schwartz f, integrate the kernel in time. For r>0, ∫0t​(4πs)−2e−r2/(4s)ds=e−r2/(4t)/(4π2r2). Consequently
v(t,x)=Pt​g(x)+4π21​∫R4​∣x−y∣2e−∣x−y∣2/(4t)​f(y)dy.​
(56)
The forcing term converges by dominated convergence to W(x)=(4π2∣⋅∣2)−1∗f. Its singularity is locally integrable in four dimensions, and the Schwartz decay controls infinity. The supplied fundamental solution identity gives −ΔW=f, first in distributions and then classically by regularity.
The asserted large-time limit is not guaranteed for arbitrary bounded smooth g. Take f=0 and g(x)=(1+∣x∣2)i, which is smooth and has modulus one. For a standard four-dimensional Gaussian Z,
Pt​g(0)=tiE[(t−1+2∣Z∣2)i]∼4iΓ(2+i)ti.
(57)
Dominated convergence gives the asymptotic, and the gamma factor is nonzero. The phase logt rotates indefinitely, so there is no limit. This is an example of heat evolution of bounded data need not converge at large times.
Under the natural additional assumption g∈C0​(R4), Pt​g→0: split the convolution into a large ball, whose heat-kernel mass tends to zero, and its complement, where g is uniformly small. Then w=W and −Δw=f. More generally, if g(x)→L at spatial infinity, the limit is w=L+W, satisfying the same equation. These are the intended qualified stationary-limit conclusions.

c OurBigBook.com
A simple zero at ip supplies a discrete scattering mode and hence an order-one, right-moving soliton component of speed 4p2. Its position depends on the associated norming constant and, for general scattering data, the appropriate scattering phase shifts. A simple zero alone does not specify its position, nor exclude additional zeros and therefore additional solitons.
To locate the continuous radiation, set ξ=x/t. The real-axis oscillatory phase is t(2kξ+8k3), whose stationary points satisfy 2ξ+24k2=0. For ξ<0 there are two real stationary points k=±−ξ/12​, giving dispersive oscillatory radiation, ordinarily of order t−1/2 for nondegenerate data. For ξ>0 there is no real stationary point, so radiation is smaller and a soliton dominates near its moving centre. At ξ=0 the stationary points merge and the natural transition scale is x=O(t1/3), with Airy-type radiation of order t−1/3. These statements assume the regular decaying scattering data implicit in the reconstruction problem; vanishing reflection can remove the radiation entirely. The discrete mode travels right, while the leading continuous radiation occupies left-going rays.

Expand a perturbed eigenvector and energy as ψ=ψ0​+λψ1​+O(λ2) and E(λ)=E+λδ+O(λ2). At first order, (H−E)ψ1​+(V−δ)ψ0​=0. Projecting onto the E eigenspace eliminates the first term and gives PE​VPE​ψ0​=δψ0​. Thus degenerate perturbation theory diagonalizes the restriction of V to that eigenspace; in the nondegenerate case this reduces to its expectation value.
For the specified two-dimensional eigenspace, the restricted matrix is (αβ​βα​). Its eigenvectors are (∣1⟩±∣2⟩)/2​ and its eigenvalues α±β. Hence the perturbed energies are E+λ(α±β)+O(λ2).
The square-box unperturbed energies are Epq​=π2ℏ2(p2+q2)/(2ma2). Every diagonal matrix element of xy/a2 is 1/4, because each coordinate has mean a/2. The ground state is (p,q)=(1,1), giving E11​+λ/4. The first excited eigenspace is spanned by (1,2) and (2,1). Its off-diagonal entry factors into the square of
∫01​2ssin(πs)sin(2πs)ds=∫01​s[cos(πs)−cos(3πs)]ds=−9π216​.

There is a genuine periodicity mismatch in the source. Write xs​=sb+us​. The intended periodic displacements in a harmonic chain satisfy uN​=u0​, equivalently xN​=x0​+Nb for unwrapped positions. The printed xN​=x0​ instead makes the potential 21​mλ2∑s​(xs+1​−xs​)2+21​Nmλ2b2, with equilibrium at equal positions, not xs​=sb. The following lattice derivation uses periodic displacements, as required by the requested position operator.
Put kr​=2πr/(Nb), r=0,…,N−1, and Fourier transform the displacements and momenta with normalization N−1/2. The spring quadratic form is diagonal, with factor ∣eikr​b−1∣2=4sin2(kr​b/2). Thus each nonzero mode is a harmonic oscillator with
ωr​=2λ∣sin(kr​b/2)∣.​
(65)
Creation and annihilation operators obey [ar​,ar′†​]=δrr′​. Inverting the oscillator-coordinate expansion gives
xs​=sb+2mNℏ​​r=0∑​ωr​​ar​eikr​sb+ar†​e−ikr​sb​.​
(66)
The conjugate momentum is ps​=−imℏ/(2N)​∑r=0​ωr​​(ar​eikr​sb−ar†​e−ikr​sb). Fourier orthogonality diagonalizes the Hamiltonian as ∑r=0​ℏωr​(ar†​ar​+1/2). The normalized oscillator vacuum is annihilated by every ar​; applying creation operators gives number states, each added phonon contributing ℏωr​. The omitted zero mode is a free centre-of-mass coordinate, which must be fixed or treated separately rather than assigned an oscillator vacuum. Accordingly the reduced displacement commutator is [us​,pt​]=iℏ(δst​−1/N).
For iqus​, separate creation and annihilation parts. Their commutator is a scalar, so the supplied Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff formula and vacuum expectations give
⟨0∣eiqus​∣0⟩=e−W(q),W(q)=4mNq2ℏ​∑r=0​ωr​1​.
(67)
Summing the geometric lattice phases yields
M=e−W(q)eiqb(N−1)/2sin(qb/2)sin(Nqb/2)​,∣M∣2=e−2W(q)[sin(qb/2)sin(Nqb/2)​]2.​
(68)
The ratio is interpreted by continuity at its removable singularities. The interference factor has its maximum N2 at q=2πn/b, where all lattice phases coincide. The source's Fourier-sum hint should read r≡0(modN), rather than r=Nb.
The claim about the full matrix element also needs qualification: its Debye–Waller factor envelope varies with q. The absolute global maximum is ∣M(0)∣2=N2; at nonzero reciprocal-lattice points the value is N2e−2W(2πn/b)<N2. Moreover the derivative of the envelope there is nonzero, whereas that of the interference factor is zero, so those points are not exact local maxima of the full finite-chain intensity. The reciprocal-lattice condition maximizes the interference factor, which is the usual constructive-scattering interpretation of the requested result.

The chemical potential is μ=(∂E/∂N)S,V​, equivalently (∂F/∂N)T,V​: it is the free-energy cost of adding a particle at fixed temperature and volume. With units kB​=1, a large reservoir has entropy SR​(Etot​−E,Ntot​−N)=SR0​−E/T+μN/T to first order. Since the number of compatible reservoir states is proportional to its exponential, the grand canonical ensemble assigns
Pr(state j,N)=Ξ−1e−(Ej,N​−μN)/T,Ξ=N,j∑​e−(Ej,N​−μN)/T.​
(69)
For independent fermions, a one-particle state of energy ε has occupation zero or one. Its partition factor is 1+e−(ε−μ)/T, so the mean occupation is the Fermi-Dirac distribution [e(ε−μ)/T+1]−1. Multiplication by the given density of states yields dN=Cε1/2dε/[e(ε−μ)/T+1].
At zero temperature the occupation is a step function, filled below μ and empty above it, so μ=εF​ and N=(2C/3)εF3/2​. At fixed particle number, the low-temperature shift of μ is O(T2/εF​) and does not affect the leading estimate. In the narrow interval of width T above εF​, replace the density of states by CεF​​ and put u=(ε−εF​)/T. Then
N>εF​​∼CεF​​T∫0∞​eu+1du​=CεF​​Tlog2.​
(70)
Equivalently, the fraction above the Fermi energy is asymptotic to (3log2/2)T/εF​.

ω2=c02​[k2+a2π2​(m2+n2)].​

Expand the prescribed entrance pressure in this cosine basis, with coefficients Amn​. Impose outgoing propagation and decay at infinity, with no incoming disturbance. At ω=ωmin​/2, only the constant transverse mode propagates, with k00​=π/(2a). All other modes have k=iχmn​, where χmn​=πm2+n2−1/4​/a. The exact modal field is the outgoing constant mode plus ∑m+n>0​Amn​cos(mπx/a)cos(nπy/a)e−χmn​z−iωt.

Words: 153 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 153
b OurBigBook.com
The Dahlquist equivalence theorem states that a linear multistep method is convergent for well-posed sufficiently smooth initial-value problems, with consistent starting values, if and only if it is consistent and zero-stable. Zero-stability means that every root of its first characteristic polynomial lies in the closed unit disk, with roots on the unit circle simple.
Here the characteristic polynomials are
ρ(z)=z3+(2a−3)z2−(2a−3)z−1=(z−1)[z2+2(a−1)z+1],σ(z)=a(z2+z).
(79)
Consistency holds because ρ(1)=0 and ρ′(1)=σ(1)=2a. The two remaining roots have product one. For 0<a<2 they are distinct conjugate unit roots, and neither equals one. At a=0, the root one is triple; at a=2, the root minus one is double. Outside [0,2], the remaining roots are real reciprocal roots and one has modulus greater than one. Thus
convergence holds exactly for 0<a<2.​
(80)
The order conditions give c2​=0 and c3​=6−a, which is nonzero throughout the convergent range. Therefore the order of convergence is exactly two, for starting approximations of matching accuracy.
